title: Wildfire smoke
summary: Keep smoke out of the house and limit your time in it, especially with diabetes, asthma or heart disease.

items.text: Watch for air quality alerts (AirNow.gov). Use several alert methods, such as the FEMA app and Wireless Emergency Alerts.
Pick a room that can be sealed from outside air. Keep its doors and windows closed.
Have a portable air cleaner ready for smoky conditions.
Keep an N95 mask on hand, if you can.
Make sure everyone knows what to do for a quick evacuation. Learn your routes and practice with the pets.
Keep supplies in a go bag or the car trunk, including a first aid kit. Keep your phone charged.

items.note: AirNow's Fire and Smoke Map shows fires and smoke across North America.

items.text: If authorities order an evacuation, **leave immediately**.
No evacuation order but smoky? Stay indoors in a safe location, or go to a community building where smoke levels are lower.
Use the closed-off room with a portable air cleaner or filter.
If your central air has high-efficiency filters, set it to "recirculate" and close the outdoor air intake damper, if it has one.
Outside, wear an N95 or limit your exposure to smoke.
items.note: NIOSH-approved respirators are not made in sizes for very young children. A poorly fitting mask does little.

items.text: People with asthma, COPD, diabetes or heart disease need extra attention in smoky air.
items.note: If you are sick and need care, contact your healthcare provider for instructions.

items.text: **Do not return home until authorities say it is safe.**
Avoid hot ash, charred trees, smoldering debris and live embers.
items.note: The ground may have heat pockets that cause burns or new fires.

items.text: For cleanup, wear a long-sleeved shirt, long pants, work gloves and sturdy thick-soled shoes. Wet debris to reduce dust.
Use text messages to reach family. Save phone calls for emergencies.
